headline: Great Point Rip: Terns Working Blues Hard, Albies Still Playing Games
subhead: Bluefish have committed on the Sound's rips while the albies tease at the edges — and the bonito push west is finally close enough to matter.
body_markdown:
Stood at the Great Point rip Tuesday morning watching a hundred terns work a bait ball the size of a pickup truck, diving so hard some of them were going under. Under that was blitzing bluefish, slashing bunker peanuts into confetti on the ebb. No albies busting through the middle of it — not that morning. That's been the story of the Sound the last ten days: the blues are locked in and violent, the albies are around but noncommittal, and everybody's watching the calendar for the bonito to finally show up in numbers.

We flagged this last week — said the bluefish would stay aggressive and widespread right through Labor Day week, and that's exactly what's playing out. Warm water in the low-to-mid 70s across the Sound has kept them fired up on peanut bunker and sand eels from Great Point down through Monomoy, and the reports out of the fleet match what the Canal and Montauk crowd are seeing too. This isn't a finicky bite. Bluefish to eight and nine pounds are hitting fast-retrieved metal — Deadly Dick or a 2-ounce Kastmaster in the epoxy jig finish — and topwater poppers when they're up busting on the surface, which has been most mornings on the last two hours of the ebb at Great Point and along the Sankaty side when the current stacks bait against the beach.

The albies are the frustrating part, and it's worth being straight about it: they're here, but they're not fully committed. Boats working Monomoy Rip and the water off Chatham are marking fish and getting shots, but the bite has been start-stop — a pod comes up, feeds for ninety seconds on something microscopic, and vanishes. That tells you they're likely tucked into bay anchovies or tiny silversides rather than committing hard to bigger forage, which is why the standard 00 Deadly Dick and Albie Snax have been outfished lately by smaller profile stuff — half-ounce epoxy jigs, small Game On Chick minnows, or a size 2 Clouser on the fly for the guys working the rips out of a skiff. If you're marking fish and getting refused on a 3-inch lure, cut down to something closer to 1.5 inches before you give up on the spot.

Bonito are the story to watch over the next week. They've been thick at Block Island and Point Judith and are pushing west into the Race and Fishers Island Sound, which puts them within realistic striking distance of Nantucket Sound proper. Historically when that push gets rolling this time of year, Nantucket Shoals and the water off Great Point start seeing scattered bonito mixed in with the albie pods within a week to ten days. Worth keeping a rod rigged with smaller Deadly Dicks or green machine feathers just in case that shows up sooner than expected — bonito this far into the run tend to be just as fussy about profile size as the albies have been.

Striped bass are around but staged, not blitzing, which tracks with what's happening up and down the coast right now. Bunker schools are still building rather than fully concentrated, and until that tightens up — which the building moon toward full on September 6-7 should help with — the bass are going to keep feeding more on structure and current edges than on the surface in big showy blitzes. Horseshoe Shoal has been holding fish on the drop of the tide, working sand eels and small bunker over the humps in 15 to 25 feet. Bucktails in the 1-ounce range tipped with a strip of squid or a white Gulp swimming mullet have been the better producer there over straight metal, worked slow along bottom on the last two hours of the ebb. Monomoy's outer rips are still worth a pass on the southwest wind — that wind stacks bait against the elbow and pushes current hard through the cut, and bass have been sitting under the blitzing blues picking off cripples on bucktail and umbrella rig drops.

Black sea bass remain the most dependable structure bite in the whole zone right now. The stretch between Craigville and Osterville has been holding fish consistently over rock and mussel bottom in 20 to 35 feet, and kayak guys working that inshore structure have been doing just as well as the boat fleet — jigs tipped with squid strips or a Gulp swimming mullet on a light jighead, fished tight to bottom on the slower stages of the tide. Fluke, by contrast, are on their expected early-September fade. The doormats have mostly cleared out of the back-bay structure for deeper ocean-side bottom, and while there are still fish to be had around Monomoy's deeper holes, the numbers are thinning fast and this isn't the bite to plan a trip around anymore.

Looking at the next few days: wind stays manageable, tides are building toward the full moon push, and that stronger flow should start tightening up the bait and forcing some decisions out of both the albies and the bass. If the first real cool front of the season slides through behind that moon — which is the thing to watch on the forecast — expect the bluefish to stay locked in, the bass to get more aggressive on the rips as bait concentrates, and a real shot at the bonito at Great Point and the Shoals before Labor Day closes out. Best bet for the next 48 hours: work the ebb at Great Point early for blues and shots at albies, then swing down to Monomoy on the afternoon southwest wind for the rip bite underneath the birds.
